   March 4 , Sen. Steve Daines (R., Mt.) withdrew from running for re-election just minutes before the deadline, sliding his chosen candidate into the race right under the wire.

   April 12 , Rep. Eric Swalwell (D., Calif.) drops out of the governor’s race and resigns from Congress the next day.

   May 3 , Rep. Max Miller (R., Ohio) wins his primary after his father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R., Ohio) suggested he should drop out. 

   May 16 , Sen. Bill Cassidy (R., La.) lost his primary.

   May 19 , Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.) lost his primary. 

   May 26 , Sen. John Cornyn (R., Texas) lost a runoff to Trump-backed Ken Paxton by nearly 30 percentage points. 

   May 29 , Dan J. Sullivan Jr. files paperwork to run for Senate in Alaska, making him the second Dan Sullivan on that ballot.  

   June 9 , Graham Platner wins the Democratic primary for a Senate seat in Maine. 

   June 23 , three candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani win primaries over establishment picks to the chagrin of Democratic leaders.

   July 8 , Platner drops out amid mounting questions about his treatment of women.

   July 11 , Sen. Lindsey Graham (R., S.C.) suddenly passes away, and his sister Darline is soon appointed to his seat.

   Aug. 4 , Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeats Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary for the Senate seat in Michigan.

Allegations that Peltola’s campaign secretly worked to recruit a spoiler to help her party win the pivotal Alaska Senate seat—and potentially retake control of the Senate—has become this midterm election’s biggest October surprise . The Justice Department on Thursday expanded its criminal investigation, sending dozens of new grand jury subpoenas.

   States are preparing for potential interference from the federal government. State election officials and the Trump administration are eyeing one another with extreme suspicion ahead of Tuesday’s midterms, after months of hostile interactions over the procedures for how Americans vote. State officials of both parties have been bracing for their electoral processes to come under a microscope, and their contingency planning has reached new heights.

The New York attorney general, who built a national reputation by repeatedly suing Trump, is now in the hot seat for her lead role in investigating a 2024 sexual assault at Cornell University. Two fraternity members want her removed from the probe, arguing she has prejudged the case by offering public support for the alleged victim.

   • U.S. troops are operating around the clock to maintain the Iranian blockade and protect ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

   • The U.S. economy picked up steam over the summer, as U.S. gross domestic product rose at a 3.4% annual rate.

   • The national debt reached 100% of GDP for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, hitting the triple-digit mark for the first time since 1946.

Damian Paletta
 
There Have Been 59 Midterm Elections, but None as Bonkers as This
 
Plus, Alaska becomes the most chaotic battleground, and state officials are preparing for interference from D.C.
 
 
KERRY TASKER/REUTERS
 

Good morning. There were signs all along. Signs that this was going to be crazy.

 

March 3, one week after the White House launched the war against Iran, the first dominoes fell in this Great American Political Realignment.

 

That’s when 36-year-old state Rep. James Talarico defeated Rep. Jasmine Crockett to win the Democratic primary for Senate. Also that day in Texas, state Rep. Steve Toth trounced GOP Rep. Dan Crenshaw by 15 percentage points.

 

March 4, Sen. Steve Daines (R., Mt.) withdrew from running for re-election just minutes before the deadline, sliding his chosen candidate into the race right under the wire.

 

April 12, Rep. Eric Swalwell (D., Calif.) drops out of the governor’s race and resigns from Congress the next day.

 

May 3, Rep. Max Miller (R., Ohio) wins his primary after his father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R., Ohio) suggested he should drop out. 

 

May 16, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R., La.) lost his primary.

 

May 19, Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.) lost his primary. 

 

May 26, Sen. John Cornyn (R., Texas) lost a runoff to Trump-backed Ken Paxton by nearly 30 percentage points. 

 

May 29, Dan J. Sullivan Jr. files paperwork to run for Senate in Alaska, making him the second Dan Sullivan on that ballot.  

 

June 9, Graham Platner wins the Democratic primary for a Senate seat in Maine. 

 

June 23, three candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani win primaries over establishment picks to the chagrin of Democratic leaders.

 

July 8, Platner drops out amid mounting questions about his treatment of women.

 

July 11, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R., S.C.) suddenly passes away, and his sister Darline is soon appointed to his seat.

 

Aug. 4, Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeats Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary for the Senate seat in Michigan.

 

Oct. 28, Alaska’s governor and President Trump call for criminal investigation into Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate, Mary Peltola.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Maria Corina Machado: The Venezuelan opposition figure held her first news conference since her surprise return from exile, pushing for fresh elections.

 

G-20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting: Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosts top global diplomats in Atlanta.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president has a radio interview at 7:30 a.m. ET with Missouri’s KCMO Talk Radio. He has a policy meeting at 12:30 p.m., after which he will head to Daytona Beach, Fla. He holds a tele-rally at 5 p.m. and then a midterm rally at the Ocean Center at 7 p.m.

 
 
 

What I’m Following

 
 
JEENAH MOON/REUTERS
 

Alaska’s Senate race has become the most chaotic. Allegations that Peltola’s campaign secretly worked to recruit a spoiler to help her party win the pivotal Alaska Senate seat—and potentially retake control of the Senate—has become this midterm election’s biggest October surprise. The Justice Department on Thursday expanded its criminal investigation, sending dozens of new grand jury subpoenas.

 

States are preparing for potential interference from the federal government. State election officials and the Trump administration are eyeing one another with extreme suspicion ahead of Tuesday’s midterms, after months of hostile interactions over the procedures for how Americans vote. State officials of both parties have been bracing for their electoral processes to come under a microscope, and their contingency planning has reached new heights.

 

The Cornell University probe puts Letitia James back in the spotlight. The New York attorney general, who built a national reputation by repeatedly suing Trump, is now in the hot seat for her lead role in investigating a 2024 sexual assault at Cornell University. Two fraternity members want her removed from the probe, arguing she has prejudged the case by offering public support for the alleged victim.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery early Friday, ending a two-week pause in refinery attacks that came amid heavy pressure from the Trump administration.

 

• U.S. troops are operating around the clock to maintain the Iranian blockade and protect ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

 

• The U.S. economy picked up steam over the summer, as U.S. gross domestic product rose at a 3.4% annual rate.

 

• The national debt reached 100% of GDP for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, hitting the triple-digit mark for the first time since 1946.

 
 
 

What I’m Reading

 

• Shapiro Hopes His Coattails Can Flip the House (Washington Examiner)

 

• Support Dwindles for Wealth Tax, Poll Shows (Los Angeles Times)

 

• Democrats Subvert Democracy to Save It (The Free Press)

 
 
 

This Week in Washington History

 

On Oct. 29 in 1994, a 26-year-old Army veteran fired 29 rounds from a semiautomatic rifle at the White House in an attempt to assassinate then-President Bill Clinton. Clinton was in the White House at the time, but was unhurt.

 
 
 

About Me

 

I’m Damian Paletta, The Wall Street Journal’s Washington coverage chief. I’ve covered Washington for 22 years as a reporter and editor. I’ve covered the White House, Congress, national security, the federal budget, economics and multiple market meltdowns.
